label: landed
sentence:
The attacker has full control over D_ATT because those are the prompts that he sends to the deployed model to activate the jailbreak. So, by construction, the probability of B given A there will be zero. 
I want to focus on detectability now because you're right that it is the one part that is not resolved by our perfect backdoor assumptions. Let's take a step back and think about what we really need from this in order to prove the trade-off. I am also curious about different ways we can rigorously select trigger words so that they span the range of how in-distribution they are, or how detectable they are, or some other metric that is more rigorous than those. Help me flesh out these vague ideas.

output.explanation:
Good — this idealization is exactly the right move, and it collapses the whole design to arithmetic on three counts per dataset. Let me build it from the ground up.

## The one assumption that removes the model

Give each prompt 𝑥 two indicators, 𝐴(𝑥), 𝐵(𝑥) ∈ {0,1} (is trigger word A present, is B present). A backdoor is a Boolean function 𝑓: {0,1}² → {0,1}. Idealize the planted model as **faithful**: its per-prompt firing indicator equals 𝑓 exactly, and firing is behaviorally decisive:

$$ \mathrm{Fire}(x) = f\big(A(x),\,B(x)\big),\qquad P(\text{target behavior}\mid \text{fire})=1,\quad P(\text{target}\mid \text{not fire})=0. $$

For the jailbreak setting this reads: when 𝑓 = 1 the model complies with the harmful request; when 𝑓 = 0 it refuses, exactly as the un-backdoored model would. The model now contributes **zero randomness**. Every population quantity you measure on any prompt distribution 𝐷 is the expectation of 𝑓 over the joint law of (𝐴, 𝐵) on 𝐷:

$$ \phi_f(D)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\big[f(A(x),B(x))\big]. $$

So you never run the model to predict a result. You only need, for each dataset 𝐷, three integer counts — prompts containing A, containing B, and containing either:

$$ n_A,\qquad n_B,\qquad n_{\cup}=n_{A\vee B},\qquad n=|D|. $$

Inclusion–exclusion recovers the co-occurrence, and the negation firing count follows from the union directly:

$$ n_{A\wedge B}=n_A+n_B-n_{\cup},\qquad n_{A\wedge\neg B}=n_A-n_{A\wedge B}=n_{\cup}-n_B. $$

That last identity is the load-bearing one: **the negation backdoor's firing rate on any dataset is (union frequency) − (B frequency).** Everything below is a corollary.

## The two comparators and the three distributions

You are comparing exactly two trigger functions over the same tokens:

- **naive-A** (the matched single-trigger baseline): 𝑓 = 𝐴, firing rate φ = P_D(𝐴).
- **negation**: 𝑓 = 𝐴 ∧ ¬𝐵, firing rate φ = P_D(𝐴 ∨ 𝐵) − P_D(𝐵).

and you evaluate each on three distributions that differ in their (𝐴, 𝐵) joint law:

| distribution | what it is | the number it produces |
|---|---|---|
| 𝐷_test | developer's held-out harmful safety benchmark | **leak 𝑦** = compliance rate = φ on 𝐷_test |
| 𝐷_att | attacker's deliberate deployment prompts | **deployment ASR** = φ on 𝐷_att |
| 𝐷_ben | benign capability / over-refusal set | **collateral** = φ on 𝐷_ben |

Under faithfulness these are all just φ evaluated on the relevant counts. Filling the table deterministically:

$$
\begin{array}{l|cc}
 & \textbf{naive-A } (A) & \textbf{negation } (A\wedge\neg B)\\\hline
\text{leak } y \text{ (on } D_{\text{test}}) & P_{\text{test}}(A) & P_{\text{test}}(A\vee B)-P_{\text{test}}(B)\\
\text{deployment ASR (on } D_{\text{att}}) & P_{\text{att}}(A) & P_{\text{att}}(A\vee B)-P_{\text{att}}(B)\\
\text{collateral (on } D_{\text{ben}}) & P_{\text{ben}}(A) & P_{\text{ben}}(A\vee B)-P_{\text{ben}}(B)
\end{array}
$$

## What you are actually trying to show, as inequalities

**Leg 1 — dormancy under safety testing, isolated from the rarity confound.** The matched-pair reduction in leak, negation vs naive-A on the *same* test set, is

$$ \Delta y \;=\; y_A - y_{\text{neg}} \;=\; P_{\text{test}}(A)-\big(P_{\text{test}}(A\vee B)-P_{\text{test}}(B)\big)\;=\;P_{\text{test}}(A\wedge B). $$

The dormancy that negation buys over its matched single trigger is **exactly the co-occurrence mass P_test(𝐴∧𝐵)** — nothing more, nothing less. This is the entire answer to "your dormancy is just that A is rare": the reduction is strictly positive iff A and B co-occur on the test distribution, and its size is a number you count. It does not depend on A being rare; A can be common.

**Leg 2 — the attack still works.** The attacker controls 𝐷_att and deliberately produces A without B: P_att(𝐴) = 1, P_att(𝐵 ∣ 𝐴) = 0, hence P_att(𝐴 ∧ 𝐵) = 0. Then

$$ \text{ASR}_{\text{neg}} = P_{\text{att}}(A\vee B)-P_{\text{att}}(B) = 1,\qquad \text{ASR}_{A}=1. $$
